title: Secret and Key Management: Why Credentials Need Different Handling Than Config
objective: Recognize why credentials and keys need handling distinct from ordinary configuration, and apply the core practices -- centralized storage, runtime injection, rotation, and scoped access -- that keep a single leaked secret from becoming total compromise.

content_blocks.heading: A Secret Isn't Just Another Config Value
content_blocks.body:
Most configuration -- a feature flag, a timeout value, a log level -- is low-stakes if it leaks: at worst it reveals how a system is tuned. A secret is categorically different: an API key, a database password, or a cloud credential grants whoever holds it the same access the legitimate system has, immediately and completely, the moment it's exposed. There's no partial compromise -- a leaked secret is a leaked identity.

That asymmetry is why secrets management is treated as its own discipline rather than folded into general configuration management. OWASP's Secrets Management Cheat Sheet frames the goal plainly: minimize the chance a secret is ever exposed, and minimize the damage when -- not if -- one eventually is anyway.

This session covers the practices that follow from treating secrets as a distinct, higher-stakes category: where they live, how services get them, and how exposure gets bounded when it happens.

content_blocks.heading: The Recurring Failure: Credentials Living in Source Control
content_blocks.body:
The single most common way secrets leak is also the simplest: a developer commits a real credential directly into source code, often just to get something working quickly, intending to remove it later. Uber's 2016 breach followed exactly this pattern -- an AWS credential was left inside code in a private GitHub repository. The repository being private didn't save it: the account lacked multi-factor authentication, an intruder obtained access to the repository itself, and from there simply read the credential out of the code like any other file.

The lesson isn't "use a more private repository" -- it's that source control, public or private, is the wrong place for a live credential at all. A repository's access controls are designed for managing who can read and change code, not for safeguarding something that grants direct access to production systems the moment it's read.

It's worth noting this pattern isn't specific to Uber or to GitHub specifically -- it recurs across companies and across every major hosting platform, precisely because committing a working credential is the fastest way to get code running locally, and removing it later requires remembering to do so before anyone else, or any automated scanner, reads the commit history first.

reference_links.label: The Register -- Uber quit GitHub for custom code after 2016 data breach

exercises.prompt: Uber's 2016 breach involved an AWS credential committed into a *private* GitHub repository. Why didn't the repository being private prevent the breach?

options: Repository access controls govern who can read code, not who can use a credential once someone reaches it
Private repositories on GitHub have never actually encrypted their stored file contents at all
The credential was leaked through a separate, fully unrelated channel, making the repository's privacy irrelevant
AWS credentials are specifically designed to work even without any repository access being needed at all
definition.explanation: The repository's privacy setting controls who can read the code -- once an intruder gained access to the repository itself (helped by the account lacking MFA), the credential sitting in that code was exposed just like any other file content. Privacy settings on a code repository were never designed to protect a live production credential.

content_blocks.heading: The Fix: Centralize, Then Inject at Runtime
content_blocks.body:
The standard practice a dedicated secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, and similar tools all follow the same shape) enables is simple to state: secrets live in exactly one centrally-managed store, and services retrieve them at runtime rather than having them baked into source code or container images. A service starts up, authenticates to the secrets manager using its own scoped identity, and pulls the specific secrets it needs into memory or environment variables -- the secret itself never touches a git commit, a Docker image layer, or a build artifact that outlives the running process.

This also makes secrets independently auditable and revocable: a centralized store can log every access, and a compromised secret can be revoked and rotated in one place without hunting through every repository and image that might have embedded a copy of it.

The tooling differs -- Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, and cloud-native equivalents all vary in setup and integration details -- but the shape of the practice is the same across all of them: one authoritative store, scoped retrieval at runtime, and no durable copy of the secret living anywhere outside it.

exercises.prompt: A team bakes a database password directly into their application's Docker image at build time, versus a team whose image pulls the same password from a secrets manager at container startup. What's the key operational difference?

options: The baked-in password persists in every image layer and build artifact; the injected one never does
There's no real difference -- both approaches store the password in the exact same way once the container is running
The injected approach is slower at runtime but otherwise provides no meaningful security improvement at all
Baking the password into the image is actually the more secure approach, since nothing external needs to be reachable
definition.explanation: A password baked into an image layer persists in every copy of that image -- registries, caches, old builds still lying around -- long after the password might need to change. Pulling it from a secrets manager at startup means the secret exists only in the running process's memory, and revoking or rotating it doesn't require rebuilding or hunting down old images.

content_blocks.heading: Rotation: Bounding How Long a Leak Stays Useful
content_blocks.body:
A secret that never changes is a secret whose exposure window never closes -- if it leaks once, undetected, it remains fully usable to whoever holds it indefinitely. Rotation -- periodically replacing a credential with a new one and invalidating the old -- doesn't prevent a leak, but it bounds how long any single leaked copy stays valid, which is the only defense available against a leak nobody has detected yet.

Uber's own response after the 2016 breach illustrates this directly: once the exposed AWS credential was discovered, the fix included rotating it -- replacing the credential so the copy the intruder held stopped working. Rotation handled routinely, on a schedule, rather than only reactively after a known incident, keeps that same exposure window short even when nobody yet knows a leak happened at all.

A secrets manager that supports automated rotation makes this practical at scale -- rotating a handful of credentials by hand on a schedule is tedious but feasible; rotating hundreds across dozens of services only stays sustainable when the rotation itself is automated rather than a recurring manual chore someone has to remember to run.

exercises.prompt: A credential is leaked but nobody detects it for six months. Why does routine rotation (even without knowing a leak occurred) still limit the damage?

options: Rotation invalidates the old credential on its own schedule, so the leaked copy stops working once rotation happens
Routine rotation has no effect at all unless the specific leak is already known and detected by that point
Rotation only matters for credentials that are already suspected of being compromised at the time it runs
A leaked credential remains valid forever regardless of rotation, since rotation only applies going forward from detection
definition.explanation: Rotation replaces a credential on its own schedule, independent of whether a leak has been detected. If a secret leaked and nobody noticed, the next scheduled rotation still invalidates the leaked copy -- bounding the exposure window to however often rotation runs, rather than however long it takes for anyone to notice.

content_blocks.heading: Scoping: Limiting Which Secrets a Service Can Even Read
content_blocks.body:
Centralizing secrets in one store creates a new risk if every service can read every secret in it: a single compromised service becomes a path to everything, which is the exact blast-radius problem the least-privilege IAM framing already applies to API access -- here applied to secrets themselves. The fix is the same shape: each service authenticates to the secrets manager with its own scoped identity, and that identity's policy grants read access only to the specific secrets that service actually needs, nothing broader.

A payments service compromised through an unrelated vulnerability shouldn't be able to read the secrets belonging to an entirely separate notifications service just because both happen to live in the same secrets manager. Scoping access per-service keeps a secrets manager from becoming a single store whose compromise is equivalent to compromising everything behind it at once.

exercises.prompt: A secrets manager grants every service read access to every stored secret, with no per-service scoping. What's the practical consequence if one unrelated service gets compromised?

options: The attacker can read every secret the manager holds, not just the ones the compromised service actually needed
Nothing beyond that one service is affected, since the compromise is still limited to that service's own process
Only secrets created after the compromise are at risk; everything stored beforehand stays fully protected
This specific scenario can't actually happen, since secrets managers are structurally immune to any compromise
definition.explanation: Without per-service scoping, every service's credential to the secrets manager grants the same broad read access -- so compromising any one service is equivalent to compromising the entire store. Scoping each service's access to only the secrets it actually needs bounds the blast radius to that one service's own footprint, the same logic least-privilege IAM already applies to API access.

content_blocks.heading: The Bottom Line
content_blocks.body:
A secret is a different category of configuration -- its exposure is immediate, total compromise, not a tunable setting leaking. The recurring real-world failure is a credential sitting in source control, as Uber's 2016 breach showed even inside a private repository. The fix is a consistent pattern: centralize secrets in a dedicated manager, inject them at runtime rather than baking them into code or images, rotate them routinely to bound how long any undetected leak stays useful, and scope each service's access to only the secrets it actually needs.

These same four moves -- centralize, inject, rotate, scope -- are the practical substance behind "secrets management" as a discipline, and they generalize past AWS credentials to TLS certificates, API keys, and signing keys alike. The next sessions in this module build on the scoping idea directly: TLS in transit and at rest, and network segmentation as the same least-exposure logic applied to traffic instead of credentials.
